# Electric battery (voltaic pile) (`electric_battery`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/electricity.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Electricity & electronics (`electricity`)
- Deps: helped by zinc_brass, copper_bronze, wire_drawing, sulphuric_acid
- Core idea: Two different metals in contact with salt water or dilute acid drive a continuous electric current. Stack pairs in a fixed order: copper (or silver) disc, zinc disc, cloth or pasteboard soaked in brine, then again copper, zinc, wet cloth, and so on. Each pair gives a little under one volt and the pairs add up, so 20 to 50 pairs give sparks, a tingling shock, twitching frog legs and enough voltage to split water with a separate electrolysis cell. A row of cups of brine or dilute acid, each holding a zinc and a copper strip linked cup to cup (crown of cups), does the same and is easier to keep working.
- Pitfalls:
  - The same metal on both sides, or the order of the metals reversed part of the way up the pile: the pairs cancel
  - Cloth that is dry, or so wet that brine runs down the side and short-circuits the pile
  - Expecting it to last: the pile weakens within minutes to hours as gas collects on the copper and the cloth dries, and the zinc is eaten away
  - Assuming zinc is at hand: before about 1600 metallic zinc is hardly known in Europe (it is made in India and China); iron with copper, or tin with silver, works but much more weakly
  - Citing the 'Baghdad battery': there is no evidence those Parthian or Sasanian jars were electric cells
- History: europe: 1780–1791 – Galvani, frog-leg experiments (he took it for animal electricity); 1800 – Volta in Pavia and Como, pile and crown of cups, announced to the Royal Society; within weeks Nicholson and Carlisle decompose water with it
- Read:
  - Alessandro Volta, On the Electricity Excited by the Mere Contact of Conducting Substances of Different Kinds, Philosophical Transactions 90 (1800)
  - Giuliano Pancaldi, Volta: Science and Culture in the Age of Enlightenment (2003)
